Choose where to open new facilities

Source: R/location.R
locate_facilities.Rd

Chooses, among the candidate sites, where to open facilities so that the demand points are served best, by one of four classic location models. The travel times from every demand point to every site are computed with travel_time_matrix() (or taken from travel_times), so any mode, departure time and routing option of the matrix applies.

Usage

locate_facilities(
  network,
  demand,
  candidates,
  existing = NULL,
  model = "max_cover",
  n_facilities = 1L,
  cutoff = NULL,
  demand_colname = NULL,
  mode = "WALK",
  mode_egress = "WALK",
  departure_datetime = NULL,
  percentile = 50L,
  max_trip_duration = NULL,
  travel_times = NULL,
  swap = TRUE,
  min_gain = 0,
  unreachable_time = NULL,
  n_threads = Inf,
  ...
)

Arguments

network

The network of build_network(); may be NULL with travel_times.

demand

The demand points: a data.frame with id, lon and lat, or a POINT sf with an id column, and, with demand_colname, their weights.

candidates

The sites where a facility could open: a data.frame or POINT sf with id, lon, lat.

existing

The facilities already open (id, lon, lat), or NULL. Their ids may not repeat those of the candidates.

model

A string: "max_cover", "set_cover", "p_median" or "p_center".

n_facilities

How many new facilities to open. Fewer come back when no further site improves the objective. Ignored by "set_cover".

cutoff

The service standard of the covering models, in minutes: a point is covered by a site at most this far (travel time <= cutoff). Required by "max_cover" and "set_cover", NULL for the other models.

demand_colname

The name of the numeric column of demand with the weight of each point (residents, pupils...), finite and not negative; NULL for a weight of 1 each.

mode

A character vector, the transport modes (see the section "Transport modes"). Defaults to "WALK".

mode_egress

A string, the mode from the last stop to the destination: "WALK" (the default), "BICYCLE" or "CAR". Ignored without public transport.

departure_datetime

A POSIXct, the departure date and time (see the section "Date and time"). Required with public transport.

percentile

The travel-time percentile used (public transport over a time window), a whole number from 1 to 99.

max_trip_duration

The longest trip considered, in minutes. NULL: cutoff (rounded up) for the covering models, 120 for the others.

travel_times

A table of travel times to use instead of routing: from_id (demand point), to_id (site) and travel_time_pXX for the percentile (or travel_time), in minutes, as travel_time_matrix() returns it. A pair that is absent or has a missing time is unreachable; rows of other points are ignored. With it, network and the routing arguments are not used and the points need only their id.

swap

A logical: improve the greedy solution by vertex substitution (for "set_cover", drop the sites the others make redundant).

min_gain

"max_cover" stops opening sites when the best one left would cover less than this much demand.

unreachable_time

For "p_median" and "p_center", the minutes charged to a demand point that reaches no open facility. NULL: twice the longest travel time of the table.

n_threads

The number of threads (Inf: all cores).

...

Any other argument of travel_time_matrix(), by its full name: time_window, walk_speed, max_walk_time, seed and so on (not percentiles or output_dir).

Value

A list of three tables and a summary:

  • sites: the new sites, ordered by what each adds: id (with lon and lat when the candidates have them), order, marginal (demand newly covered, or by how much the objective falls) and cumulative (demand covered so far, existing facilities included, or the objective so far).

  • candidates: one row per candidate: id, potential (what it would add as the only new facility; for the covering models, the demand not covered today that it would cover alone) and chosen.

  • demand: one row per demand point: id, demand (its weight), facility_id and travel_time (the nearest open facility, existing or new, and the minutes to it; NA when it reaches none) and covered (within the cutoff of a facility; for "p_median" and "p_center", whether it reaches one).

  • summary: a list with model, n_sites, objective_before (existing facilities only), objective_greedy, objective (demand covered, number of sites, weighted minutes or largest minutes, by model), covered_before and covered (covering models, else NA), total_demand, unservable_demand (demand no site can serve) and n_swaps.

    Tables are tibbles by default; options(peabiru.output = "data.frame") gives base data.frames and options(peabiru.output = "data.table") gives data.tables (see peabiru-package).

Models

  • "max_cover", maximal covering (Church and ReVelle, 1974): with n_facilities new facilities, cover the most demand within cutoff minutes.

  • "set_cover", location set covering (Toregas et al., 1971): the fewest new facilities that leave every demand point within cutoff minutes of one (every point some site can cover; the demand of the others is reported in summary$unservable_demand).

  • "p_median" (Hakimi, 1964): n_facilities new facilities with the smallest demand-weighted sum of travel times to the nearest facility.

  • "p_center" (Hakimi, 1964): n_facilities new facilities with the smallest travel time for the demand point farthest from its nearest facility.

The existing facilities are already open and count first: only the demand they leave uncovered, or the travel time they leave, drives the choice of the new sites. They are never closed or moved.

How the models are solved

By heuristics, with no integer programming solver: a greedy construction (each site the one that improves the objective most, given the ones before it) followed, with swap, by vertex substitution (Teitz and Bart, 1968): an open new site is swapped for a closed candidate while that improves the objective, the best swap of all at each step. For "set_cover" the greedy choice is the site covering the most points not yet covered, and the improvement drops the sites the others make redundant; for "p_center" greedy and swaps compare the largest travel time and, on ties, the weighted sum. The solution is good and reproducible, not proven optimal. For maximal covering the greedy solution covers at least 63% (1 - 1/e) of the most that could be covered of the demand not yet covered (Nemhauser, Wolsey and Fisher, 1978). Ties go to the candidate listed first, and the result does not depend on n_threads.

In "set_cover" and "p_center" a demand point with weight 0 is not demand, and the others count the same whatever their weight. In "p_median" and "p_center" a demand point that reaches no open facility (within max_trip_duration) is charged unreachable_time minutes, and one that no site at all reaches is left out and reported.

References

Church R, ReVelle C (1974). "The maximal covering location problem." Papers of the Regional Science Association, 32, 101-118. doi:10.1007/BF01942293 .

Hakimi SL (1964). "Optimum locations of switching centers and the absolute centers and medians of a graph." Operations Research, 12(3), 450-459. doi:10.1287/opre.12.3.450 .

Nemhauser GL, Wolsey LA, Fisher ML (1978). "An analysis of approximations for maximizing submodular set functions-I." Mathematical Programming, 14, 265-294. doi:10.1007/BF01588971 .

Teitz MB, Bart P (1968). "Heuristic methods for estimating the generalized vertex median of a weighted graph." Operations Research, 16(5), 955-961. doi:10.1287/opre.16.5.955 .

Toregas C, Swain R, ReVelle C, Bergman L (1971). "The location of emergency service facilities." Operations Research, 19(6), 1363-1373. doi:10.1287/opre.19.6.1363 .

See also

floating_catchment() for supply against demand around each place.

Other location functions: floating_catchment()

Examples

data_path <- system.file("extdata/spo", package = "peabiru")
network <- build_network(data_path, n_threads = 2)
points <- read.csv(file.path(data_path, "spo_points.csv"))

# two new schools, so that the most residents are within a 12-minute
# walk of a school
schools <- points[points$schools > 0, ]
others <- points[points$schools == 0, ]
found <- locate_facilities(
  network, points, others, existing = schools,
  model = "max_cover", n_facilities = 2, cutoff = 12,
  demand_colname = "population", mode = "WALK", n_threads = 2
)
found$sites
#> # A tibble: 2 × 6
#>   id                lon   lat order marginal cumulative
#>   <chr>           <dbl> <dbl> <int>    <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1 89a8100c03bffff -46.6 -23.6     1     5658      43534
#> 2 89a8100c383ffff -46.6 -23.5     2     2683      46217
found$summary$covered / found$summary$total_demand
#> [1] 0.9987898
